newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Mobil Australia crude tanker hit by strike.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Mobil Australia crude tanker hit by strike.

text.p: A tanker carrying 30,000 litres of Griffin crude is being prevented by its Australian crew from being unloaded at Mobil Oil Australia Ltd's Altona refinery on Port Phillip Bay in Melbourne, Mobil said on Friday.

The tanker, chartered by a consortium of oil majors operating refineries in Australia, has been stranded at the 108,000-barrels-per-day plant since October 10 when Maritime Union of Australia (MUA) seamen refused to continue unloading.
Mobil Australia is wholly-owned by Mobil Corp.

The tanker Canopus, owned 14 percent by Mobil, had unloaded about 50,000 litres before its crew downed tools in protest at the consortium's plan to cease chartering the vessel in future, local Mobil spokeswoman Samantha Potts told Reuters.
The Canopus is being prevented from leaving Altona, tieing up the refinery wharf, but crude supplies are unaffected due to plenty of crude being in tankage at the plant, she said.
She declined to say whether pipeline supplies of Gippsland crude had been stepped up since the dispute began.

Gippsland crude, piped in from Bass Strait offshore fields owned equally by The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd and Exxon Corp unit Esso Australia Ltd, normally meets about 60 percent of the refinery's needs. The rest is shipped in.
"It's not affected production at all," Potts said.
The MUA was unavailable for comment on Friday.
Union and Mobil officials were meeting in Sydney on Friday in an effort to resolve the dispute.
Mobil has decided it is no longer viable to continue in the consortium, which charters both the Canopus and another tanker, the Era. The Era's charter is due to end in January.
Other consortium members are the Australian units of British Petroleum Co Plc and Royal Dutch/Shell and Ampol Petroleum Pty Ltd, a Mobil source told Reuters.
Mobil plans to charter its own vessels independently, using more efficient foreign-crewed tankers, Potts said.
"It's just not efficient for us to run Australian-flagged vessels and Australian crews," she said.
